# Curriculum vitae: Dr Maarja Sirelkoit

Updated 18 September 2026

## Current appointment

Associate Professor of Musicology, School of Cultural Evidence, Rannakaar University, Tartu, Estonia. Permanent appointment since September 2021; employment fraction 1.0 FTE. Coordinator of the university's Fragmentary Music Evidence team. My work concerns musical notation in damaged manuscripts, the evidential status of reconstructed readings, and the relationship between written musical sources and performed examples.

Rannakaar University is my employing institution and the custodian of the manuscript material used in our completed pilot. The team is an internal university group. My appointment includes research, teaching and collection-related service.

## Education and appointments

- 2005–2008: BA in Music Studies, Rannakaar University.
- 2008–2010: MA in Historical Musicology, Rannakaar University. Dissertation on attribution practices in unsigned domestic song manuscripts.
- 2010–2014: Doctoral researcher, Rannakaar University. PhD awarded June 2014 for *Reading musical remnants: evidential boundaries in incomplete household manuscripts*.
- September 2014–August 2017: Research Fellow in Manuscript Music, Rannakaar University.
- September 2017–August 2021: Lecturer in Musicology, Rannakaar University.
- September 2021–present: Associate Professor of Musicology, Rannakaar University.

## Research responsibilities

I was principal investigator of the university-funded project *Fragmentary Music Evidence Pilot*, award RU-CE-2024-07, from January 2024 to December 2025. I held responsibility for expenditure, access permissions, the classification protocol, performer recruitment and submission of the final report. The university accepted the report in February 2026 and closed the financial account in March 2026.

For that project I wrote the musicological annotation guide and served as one of the independent annotators. I also documented relationships between fragment identifiers, manuscript folders, image derivatives and interpretive statements. The final catalogue preserves the independent labels alongside any later commentary.

My current teaching covers source criticism, musical palaeography and documentation of editorial interventions. I have supervised completed master's dissertations involving manuscript descriptions and performance-based interpretation. I have not supervised a doctoral thesis to completion.

## Methods and contribution

My practical methods include close reading of notation, comparison of scribal habits, source description, structured annotation and qualitative analysis of reasons for disagreement. I use scripted catalogue checks prepared with colleagues. Historical language assessment is undertaken by our employed historical linguist; acoustic processing and numerical implementation are undertaken by our employed acoustic analyst.

The distinctive contribution of my work is the separation of what survives on the page from what an editor supplies. A legible note, an uncertain note, a missing passage and a plausible supplied passage have different statuses in our records. A performance of a supplied passage remains an interpretation, even when it sounds coherent.

## Research outputs and service

The accompanying publication record contains four published articles, including the jointly authored pilot methods and results paper published in July 2026. These publications concern manuscript evidence, linguistic attribution and documented audio processing.

I maintain the team's annotation vocabulary and chair its internal source-reading meetings. The university collection staff retain authority over handling and reproduction of originals.

# Final report: Fragmentary Music Evidence Pilot

Award RU-CE-2024-07, Rannakaar University Research Development Fund

Project period: 1 January 2024–31 December 2025. Final report accepted 20 February 2026. This copy incorporates the permissions and deposit status recorded on 18 September 2026; the analytical results are unchanged.

Principal investigator: Dr Maarja Sirelkoit. Team: Dr Tõnis Lehevald, historical linguistics; Kadri Vahenurm, acoustic signal processing.

## Purpose and material

The pilot examined whether incomplete musical sources could be described without concealing disagreements between readers. Its practical outputs were a linked catalogue, independent classifications, provenance records and a small set of documented performance examples.

The corpus comprised 180 score fragments from six manuscript folders, with 30 fragments selected from each folder. Collection descriptions assign the source material to approximately 1870–1935. Those dates are catalogue ranges, not independently verified dates for every leaf. Selection required permission to reproduce the fragment and enough surviving notation for an initial reading. Completely illegible leaves were therefore absent from the sample.

Each fragment received a stable identifier linked to its physical folder and leaf reference. Separate records described visible notation, surviving words, physical loss and editorial inference. Fragment identifiers refer to physical source units. Several fragments can preserve related material, and similarity between them does not establish a shared author or date.

The audio component comprised 24 consented examples performed by eight adult participants, with three examples per participant. All 24 examples are unaccompanied solo singing with underlaid text: one singer performs a single melodic line in each recording. Each deposited example lasts 45 seconds, giving 18 minutes of deposited audio. Participants performed short readings prepared from the source material. These are contemporary demonstration recordings of the team's interpretations. The deposited reading sheets distinguish surviving words and syllables from supplied text and record uncertain placement of syllables beneath notes.

## Annotation and provenance methods

Sirelkoit and Lehevald independently assigned one of three labels to each fragment: predominantly vocal, predominantly instrumental, or insufficient evidence. The guide required readers to cite visible features supporting their choice. Surviving verbal text could support a vocal classification, but its absence was not sufficient evidence of instrumental use. The insufficient-evidence label was available whenever the surviving material did not support either positive classification.

The readers entered their labels before seeing each other's decisions. Subsequent discussion was recorded separately and did not overwrite the independent records. The project did not appoint an adjudicator, assemble a gold-standard set or ask a third reader to settle disagreement. Interpretive notes distinguish a surviving inscription from an inferred language identification and distinguish both from a modern transcription.

The team completed source links and separate observation/inference fields for all 180 catalogue entries. This is a documentation-completeness result. Verification of the underlying provenance statements and classifications remained outside that check.

## Classification results

The two annotators agreed on 146 of 180 classifications, or 81.1%. A descriptive Wilson 95% confidence interval for this proportion is 74.8%–86.2%, treating fragments as independent observations. Because fragments were selected within folders and can be related, that interval does not capture all dependence or selection uncertainty and is not a population-level estimate for the whole collection.

The agreed classifications comprised 96 predominantly vocal fragments and 50 predominantly instrumental fragments. There were no cases in which both readers selected insufficient evidence. The remaining 34 fragments were disputed: 18 had vocal/instrumental disagreement, 10 had vocal/insufficient-evidence disagreement and six had instrumental/insufficient-evidence disagreement. These categories account for the entire corpus.

The 34 disputed cases remain disputed in the deposited catalogue. They are not 34 demonstrated errors, and the 146 agreements are not 146 verified correct answers. Agreement was an observed property of these two readers using this guide.

Reading meetings identified recurring reasons for disagreement, including detached verbal text, notation resembling both a sung line and an instrumental part, and uncertainty about whether marks belonged to the original writing or a later addition. These observations were qualitative explanations of particular cases. The project did not estimate their prevalence across the wider archive.

## Audio processing results

Vahenurm implemented a reproducible desktop workflow for importing the licensed recordings, retaining untouched source files, generating denoised derivatives and logging processing settings. All 24 examples passed through the workflow. The deposited audio format is mono PCM WAV at 48 kHz and 24-bit resolution. File checksums distinguish each original from its derivatives.

Noise reduction was assessed in manually marked non-performance intervals within the same recordings. The median reduction in measured noise power was 3.2 dB across 24 examples. A performer-cluster bootstrap gave a 95% interval of 2.4–4.0 dB for the median; the resampling unit was the performer, retaining the three associated examples together. With only eight performer clusters, this interval provides limited information about variation beyond these recordings.

No reference annotation of note onsets exists for any of the 24 recordings as of 18 September 2026. The interval markings identify non-performance regions only; the reading sheets have no alignment to recorded event times. Untouched recordings preserve the performed interpretations, rather than establishing the historical correctness of the readings.

This measure concerns intervals without intended performance. Note recognition, preservation of musical transients and recovery of masked material were not evaluated. Informal listening informed settings but was not a blinded perceptual evaluation. There was no held-out test set or predetermined recovery pass/fail rule. Recovery of missing material was outside the pilot's aims.

## Delivery, expenditure and limitations

The final accepted expenditure was EUR 46,800: EUR 31,200 in staff costs, EUR 6,000 in performer fees and recording-session support, EUR 4,800 in collection handling and digitisation services, and EUR 4,800 in institutional indirect costs. These amounts exhaust the award. No equipment purchase was charged to it. The internal award specified a fixed indirect-cost contribution of EUR 4,800 against EUR 42,000 in direct costs; it did not use the university's external-grant percentage rate.

The project delivered the catalogue, annotation guide, processing scripts, consent register and restricted audio deposit. The public metadata deposit contains the independent labels and provenance fields. Audio access follows the separate performer agreements.

The pilot established that the team could process and document the selected material with existing facilities. It left the central interpretive problem unresolved: plausible readings can differ even when their supporting evidence is recorded. The sample excluded the most illegible material, the performers were recruited locally, and the recordings were made for demonstration.

# Publications and associated research outputs

Fragmentary Music Evidence team, Rannakaar University

Record checked 18 September 2026. All four articles listed below are published. There are no submitted or under-review manuscripts in this record. Titles and identifiers are given as registered in the university's publication catalogue.

## Published articles

**Sirelkoit, M. (2018). Reading absence in domestic song manuscripts: a layered description protocol.** *Rannakaar Papers in Musical Evidence*, 3(1), 21–39. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-fragmentary-music-archive-team.2018.1

This single-author article separates physical description, diplomatic transcription and editorial supplementation in descriptions of incomplete musical manuscripts. Its contribution is a source-reading protocol and worked examples. It predates the pilot corpus. The protocol provided the conceptual basis for retaining visible evidence and supplied material in different catalogue fields.

**Lehevald, T., and Sirelkoit, M. (2021). Language attribution when song texts survive as isolated syllables.** *Baltic Review of Manuscript Linguistics*, 6(2), 77–96. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-fragmentary-music-archive-team.2021.2

This article examines the distinction between a readable character sequence and an attribution of that sequence to a language or dialect. It documents cases in which musical underlay, abbreviation and later handwriting prevent a secure attribution. The authors argue for preserving alternative readings with their evidence. Lehevald led the linguistic analysis; Sirelkoit analysed notation and placement of text beneath the musical line.

**Vahenurm, K., and Sirelkoit, M. (2024). Documenting denoising decisions in short performed manuscript examples.** *Journal of Annotated Sound Provenance*, 2(1), 11–28. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-fragmentary-music-archive-team.2024.3

This methods article describes retention of originals, parameter logging and reversible comparison of processed audio derivatives. It reports workflow development during the pilot's early recording work. Vahenurm implemented the processing and file-validation procedures; Sirelkoit supplied the musicological requirements and checked links to source readings. The article concerns auditable processing decisions.

**Sirelkoit, M., Lehevald, T., and Vahenurm, K. (2026). Agreement without adjudication: linked evidence for fragmentary musical sources.** *Rannakaar Papers in Musical Evidence*, 11(2), 44–68. DOI: 10.99999/pb.v2-fragmentary-music-archive-team.2026.4

Published July 2026. This is the pilot's joint results article. It reports the independent classification exercise, preservation of unresolved disagreements and linkage between source descriptions and audio derivatives. The numerical results are those in the final report; the publication is not an independent replication. Sirelkoit coordinated the study and manuscript, Lehevald co-designed and undertook annotation, and Vahenurm implemented the processing and numerical summaries. All authors reviewed the interpretation of uncertainty.

## Associated deposits

The *Fragmentary Music Evidence Pilot Catalogue*, release 1.0, is held in the Rannakaar University repository. Its public component contains catalogue metadata, independent classifications, the annotation guide and processing scripts. Its restricted component contains licensed source images, consent records and the complete audio examples.

The team's publication record establishes experience with musical source criticism, linguistic ambiguity and reproducible audio documentation.

# Facilities, holdings and permissions statement

Rannakaar University, School of Cultural Evidence

Inventory and rights status: 18 September 2026

## Existing facilities

The team has two university-owned desktop workstations, each with 32 GB RAM and a 1 TB solid-state drive. Both are operational and available through the school's ordinary research facilities allocation. The installed workflow uses Python, NumPy, SciPy and an audio editor for inspection, parameter recording and digital denoising.

A managed university file service stores the authoritative project directory, including untouched originals, versioned metadata and processed derivatives. Routine institutional backups cover this directory. The desktops hold working copies. Access to participant-linked files is limited to named team members and authorised repository staff.

The university's shared digitisation room has a copy stand, a digital camera, diffuse lighting and a book cradle suitable for the loose leaves and supported manuscript openings used in the pilot. Collection staff supervise handling and maintain the link between source identifiers and image filenames. These facilities supplied the pilot images. Their continued availability under the ordinary internal booking system is confirmed in the host letter.

The school's existing recording room, audio interface and microphone supported the contemporary performance examples. The recording chain is sufficient to replay, inspect and process the existing files. The completed corpus can be analysed as deposited.

The November 2025 facilities review recorded a supplier quotation for an overhead scanner at EUR 28,000, including delivery and VAT. The quotation was not pursued and expired in February 2026; no order was placed and the scanner was not purchased. The pilot completed its digitisation through the existing shared room.

## Source and participant permissions

The Rannakaar Manuscript and Sound Collection is an internal university collection. The university holds the physical manuscripts used in the pilot and controls access to them under its collection procedures. Custody of an object is recorded separately from permission to publish its image.

The collection director signed the pilot reproduction and publication permission on 12 June 2025. It covers the selected source images, annotated excerpts, catalogue descriptions and publication of the described pilot results. It does not automatically cover other material in the collection. The signed document is held with the source-access register.

All eight performers signed participation and use agreements before recording. The agreements cover research processing, creation of denoised and synthetically masked derivatives, and publication of the designated audio examples and related pilot findings. They exclude unrestricted redistribution of the complete recordings and voice identification or voice cloning.

The university ethics panel issued its favourable determination on 22 November 2023, before recruitment began. The determination covers secondary research analysis of the recorded examples within the terms of the participant agreements, without time limit. Recruitment and recording ended during the completed pilot. No participant withdrawal was recorded by 18 September 2026. No new recruitment is active, and there is no pending ethics application for an extension of the study.

## Host confirmation and access boundaries

The dean signed the host support statement on 15 September 2026. It confirms the team's employment, access to the existing facilities, institutional administration of research funds and stewardship of the completed pilot records. It does not commit additional posts, dedicated future staff effort or a cash contribution to an unapproved project.

The finance schedule accompanying the statement records the university's external-grant indirect-cost rate as 15% of all direct costs, including staff and internal services. Indirect costs are added to direct costs to obtain the total grant cost. This schedule has been effective since 1 January 2026. The completed internal pilot retained the fixed contribution specified in its award.

Current monthly employer costs for one full-time equivalent are EUR 4,800 for Sirelkoit's grade, EUR 4,200 for Lehevald's grade and EUR 4,000 for Vahenurm's grade. These amounts include salary and employer contributions, exclude institutional indirect costs and are prorated by charged employment fraction and duration. Vahenurm's existing 0.8 FTE appointment therefore costs EUR 3,200 per calendar month before indirect costs. Research time is charged against recorded effort; employment fractions do not establish available project effort.

The internal tariff is EUR 30 per booked room-hour for the digitisation room and EUR 45 per staff-hour for collection handling, charged separately when both are used. Room use includes the camera, lighting and cradle. Existing deposited files carry no additional digitisation charge. Workstation use and routine storage are covered by institutional indirect costs. The university's statistical consultation service charges EUR 75 per adviser-hour before indirect costs; it is available through internal booking, with no adviser or hours assigned to this team as of the statement date. Internal tariffs carry no additional VAT.

Public catalogue metadata are available under CC BY 4.0; the processing scripts are released under the MIT licence. Manuscript images and audio retain their documented access conditions. Consent forms are not public research data. External researchers can inspect the public annotation structure and scripts, but access to restricted files requires a separate decision under the repository's procedures.

The signed host statement and the pilot publication permissions are complete and in force as of this inventory date.

# Team roles and research practice

Fragmentary Music Evidence team, Rannakaar University

Statement dated 18 September 2026

## Composition and employment

The team comprises three employed researchers: Dr Maarja Sirelkoit, musicologist and coordinator; Dr Tõnis Lehevald, historical linguist; and Kadri Vahenurm, acoustic signal analyst. Sirelkoit and Lehevald each hold permanent 1.0 FTE appointments. Vahenurm holds a permanent 0.8 FTE research software and acoustics appointment. These are employment fractions across their institutional duties, not fractions already committed to another research award.

Sirelkoit is responsible for musical source criticism, interpretation of notation, coordination and accountability for research decisions. Her CV accompanies this statement. She was an annotator in the pilot.

Lehevald joined the university in September 2018 after completing a doctorate in historical linguistics at Rannakaar University in 2016. His work concerns fragmentary written Estonian, orthographic variation and language attribution from limited verbal evidence. He designed the linguistic evidence fields and was the second independent pilot annotator. His assessments record alternative readings and the limits of attribution from surviving syllables.

Vahenurm completed an MSc in acoustic signal processing at Rannakaar University in 2019, worked as a fixed-term technician in the university's media unit from 2019 to 2021, and took up her permanent research software and acoustics post in January 2022. She maintains the audio-processing scripts, checks file integrity and documents how processing choices affect derivatives. She has experience with digital filtering, spectral analysis and reproducible numerical workflows. She does not hold a doctorate.

## Collaboration and responsibilities

The university collection staff provided supervised access and digitisation services during the pilot. Repository staff administer the public and restricted deposits. These are internal service relationships. There are no external institutional partners, subcontracted research teams or signed external research collaboration agreements in the current group.

The eight performers contributed the licensed contemporary examples as participants. Their participation does not constitute an agreement to provide further recordings.

Interpretive changes require an entry explaining what evidence was reconsidered and who made the change. Original observations and independent labels remain recoverable. Vahenurm checks the technical integrity of a new deposit; Sirelkoit and Lehevald check whether its descriptions preserve the distinction between observed and inferred content.

## Established practice and limits

The team combines qualitative source reading with structured annotations and quantitative summaries. Its strongest completed evidence concerns the practicability of documenting incomplete sources and processing linked audio on ordinary desktop equipment. The unresolved classifications show that a complete catalogue record can still contain substantial interpretive uncertainty.

The existing recordings retain unprocessed references and documented licences for research transformations. The software can mix recorded audio with generated noise and retain parameters and derivative identifiers. No controlled synthetic-masking recovery study, calibrated uncertainty model or independent comparison of recovery methods has been completed.

Within the musical material, modern performances provide examples of particular readings, while the catalogue records the evidence and uncertainty behind those readings. The team retains the original audio alongside processed derivatives so that changes to acoustic features can be inspected.

# Final report: Fragmentary Music Evidence Pilot

Award RU-CE-2024-07, Rannakaar University Research Development Fund

Project period: 1 January 2024–31 December 2025. Final report accepted 20 February 2026. This copy incorporates the permissions and deposit status recorded on 18 September 2026; the analytical results are unchanged.

Principal investigator: Dr Maarja Sirelkoit. Team: Dr Tõnis Lehevald, historical linguistics; Kadri Vahenurm, acoustic signal processing.

## Purpose and material

The pilot examined whether incomplete musical sources could be described without concealing disagreements between readers. Its practical outputs were a linked catalogue, independent classifications, provenance records and a small set of documented performance examples.

The corpus comprised 180 score fragments from six manuscript folders, with 30 fragments selected from each folder. Collection descriptions assign the source material to approximately 1870–1935. Those dates are catalogue ranges, not independently verified dates for every leaf. Selection required permission to reproduce the fragment and enough surviving notation for an initial reading. Completely illegible leaves were therefore absent from the sample.

Each fragment received a stable identifier linked to its physical folder and leaf reference. Separate records described visible notation, surviving words, physical loss and editorial inference. Fragment identifiers refer to physical source units. Several fragments can preserve related material, and similarity between them does not establish a shared author or date.

The audio component comprised 24 consented examples performed by eight adult participants, with three examples per participant. All 24 examples are unaccompanied solo singing with underlaid text: one singer performs a single melodic line in each recording. Each deposited example lasts 45 seconds, giving 18 minutes of deposited audio. Participants performed short readings prepared from the source material. These are contemporary demonstration recordings of the team's interpretations. The deposited reading sheets distinguish surviving words and syllables from supplied text and record uncertain placement of syllables beneath notes.

## Annotation and provenance methods

Sirelkoit and Lehevald independently assigned one of three labels to each fragment: predominantly vocal, predominantly instrumental, or insufficient evidence. The guide required readers to cite visible features supporting their choice. Surviving verbal text could support a vocal classification, but its absence was not sufficient evidence of instrumental use. The insufficient-evidence label was available whenever the surviving material did not support either positive classification.

The readers entered their labels before seeing each other's decisions. Subsequent discussion was recorded separately and did not overwrite the independent records. The project did not appoint an adjudicator, assemble a gold-standard set or ask a third reader to settle disagreement. Interpretive notes distinguish a surviving inscription from an inferred language identification and distinguish both from a modern transcription.

The team completed source links and separate observation/inference fields for all 180 catalogue entries. This is a documentation-completeness result. Verification of the underlying provenance statements and classifications remained outside that check.

## Classification results

The two annotators agreed on 146 of 180 classifications, or 81.1%. A descriptive Wilson 95% confidence interval for this proportion is 74.8%–86.2%, treating fragments as independent observations. Because fragments were selected within folders and can be related, that interval does not capture all dependence or selection uncertainty and is not a population-level estimate for the whole collection.

The agreed classifications comprised 96 predominantly vocal fragments and 50 predominantly instrumental fragments. There were no cases in which both readers selected insufficient evidence. The remaining 34 fragments were disputed: 18 had vocal/instrumental disagreement, 10 had vocal/insufficient-evidence disagreement and six had instrumental/insufficient-evidence disagreement. These categories account for the entire corpus.

The 34 disputed cases remain disputed in the deposited catalogue. They are not 34 demonstrated errors, and the 146 agreements are not 146 verified correct answers. Agreement was an observed property of these two readers using this guide.

Reading meetings identified recurring reasons for disagreement, including detached verbal text, notation resembling both a sung line and an instrumental part, and uncertainty about whether marks belonged to the original writing or a later addition. These observations were qualitative explanations of particular cases. The project did not estimate their prevalence across the wider archive.

## Audio processing results

Vahenurm implemented a reproducible desktop workflow for importing the licensed recordings, retaining untouched source files, generating denoised derivatives and logging processing settings. All 24 examples passed through the workflow. The deposited audio format is mono PCM WAV at 48 kHz and 24-bit resolution. File checksums distinguish each original from its derivatives.

Noise reduction was assessed in manually marked non-performance intervals within the same recordings. The median reduction in measured noise power was 3.2 dB across 24 examples. A performer-cluster bootstrap gave a 95% interval of 2.4–4.0 dB for the median; the resampling unit was the performer, retaining the three associated examples together. With only eight performer clusters, this interval provides limited information about variation beyond these recordings.

No reference annotation of note onsets exists for any of the 24 recordings as of 18 September 2026. The interval markings identify non-performance regions only; the reading sheets have no alignment to recorded event times. Untouched recordings preserve the performed interpretations, rather than establishing the historical correctness of the readings.

This measure concerns intervals without intended performance. Note recognition, preservation of musical transients and recovery of masked material were not evaluated. Informal listening informed settings but was not a blinded perceptual evaluation. There was no held-out test set or predetermined recovery pass/fail rule. Recovery of missing material was outside the pilot's aims.

## Delivery, expenditure and limitations

The final accepted expenditure was EUR 46,800: EUR 31,200 in staff costs, EUR 6,000 in performer fees and recording-session support, EUR 4,800 in collection handling and digitisation services, and EUR 4,800 in institutional indirect costs. These amounts exhaust the award. No equipment purchase was charged to it. The internal award specified a fixed indirect-cost contribution of EUR 4,800 against EUR 42,000 in direct costs; it did not use the university's external-grant percentage rate.

The project delivered the catalogue, annotation guide, processing scripts, consent register and restricted audio deposit. The public metadata deposit contains the independent labels and provenance fields. Audio access follows the separate performer agreements.

The pilot established that the team could process and document the selected material with existing facilities. It left the central interpretive problem unresolved: plausible readings can differ even when their supporting evidence is recorded. The sample excluded the most illegible material, the performers were recruited locally, and the recordings were made for demonstration.
